sections.title: Mental model — escape the comparison bound deliberately

blocks.md: Contest reality: std::sort's n log n is usually fine; it stops being fine when n·log n × constant collides with brutal TLs or when the PROBLEM ITSELF is about order statistics. Then radix/counting/BIT machinery enters.
**Radix = counting sort per digit, stable so digit order accumulates correctly. LSD low→high for numbers; MSD for strings/tries-adjacent tasks.**

blocks.label: LSD radix over 16-bit digits
blocks.py:
def radix_sort(a):
    for shift in (0, 16):                     # base 2^16: two passes
        count = [0] * 65536
        for x in a: count[(x >> shift) & 0xFFFF] += 1
        total = 0
        for i in range(65536):
            count[i], total = total, total + count[i]   # positions
        tmp = [0] * len(a)
        for x in a:                           # backwards = STABLE
            d = (x >> shift) & 0xFFFF
            tmp[count[d]] = x; count[d] += 1
        a = tmp
    return a

items.q: Why backwards copy loop inside counting placement?
options: stability — equal digits keep relative input order
items.explain: Prefix sums point one-past-last; reverse fill preserves arrival order.

chain.q: Three inversion-count implementations — when does each win?
chain.a: Merge-count: no deps, cache-friendly, doubles as D&C template. BIT+compression: online/streaming variants, generalizes to distinct-range queries. pb_ds ordered_set: fastest to TYPE in contest; GCC-only. Know all three sentences cold.

chain.q: When do you hand-roll sort instead of std::sort?
chain.a: Radix when n ≥ ~10⁶ AND keys ≤ 10⁹ (2 passes beat comparisons ~3×). Counting when range tiny. Custom merge when inversion/adjacent stats needed anyway. Otherwise NEVER — std::sort is brutally tuned.
Tie-chain strictly: `if (a.k != b.k) return a.k < b.k; return tiebreak(a,b);` Never `<=`; test equal-key floods before submitting — hacked comparators are RE (runtime error) farms.

chain.q: Sorting pairs by second element fast?
chain.a: `sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [&](auto&a, auto&b){ return a.second < b.second; })` or store inverted pairs and rely on default pair-ordering — zero-comparator trick keeps code short under pressure.

items.statement: Implement all three engines; benchmark on n=10⁵ random + sorted inputs; report which wins where.

BIT needs compression — reuse Foundations L4 snippet.

solutionCode.label: merge-count and Fenwick-rank engines side by side

items.complexity: All three are O(n log n). Merge has the best constants and no compression step; Fenwick is fastest when values are already small; a policy tree is the shortest to write but carries the heaviest per-node overhead.

followups.q: Which engine wins on already-sorted input?
followups.a: Merge sort still does its full n log n of work — the split is positional and cannot detect order, though the "skip the merge if a[mid-1] <= a[mid]" guard makes it near-linear in practice. Fenwick does the same work regardless. On random data the merge version is usually fastest because it is sequential and cache-friendly, while the BIT jumps around memory in a bit-reversal pattern.

followups.q: When does compression cost more than it saves?
followups.a: Compression is a sort plus a unique plus n binary searches — effectively a second n log n pass before the BIT even starts. If the values are already small and bounded (say heights ≤ 100), skip it and index the BIT directly. Compression only pays when the value range dwarfs n.

items.title: Radix Sort Showdown
items.statement: Sort 5×10⁶ uniform uint32 with std::sort AND LSD radix (base 2¹⁶); time both; explain crossover point.
hints: Two passes only — see section code.
Uniform data favors radix; adversarial skew narrows gap.

solutionCode.label: two-pass LSD radix on 32-bit keys, base 65536
solutionCode.py:
def radix_sort(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """Two-pass LSD radix on 32-bit unsigned keys, base 65536."""
    BITS, BUCKETS = 16, 1 << 16
    MASK = BUCKETS - 1
    a = a[:]
    for shift in (0, 16):
        count = [0] * (BUCKETS + 1)
        for x in a:
            count[((x >> shift) & MASK) + 1] += 1
        for b in range(BUCKETS):
            count[b + 1] += count[b]          # prefix sums
        tmp = [0] * len(a)
        for x in a:
            idx = (x >> shift) & MASK
            tmp[count[idx]] = x               # STABLE scatter
            count[idx] += 1
        a = tmp
    return a

items.complexity: LSD radix base 2^16 sorts 32-bit keys in exactly 2 passes: O(2(n + 65536)) = O(n). std::sort is O(n log n) ≈ 22n comparisons at n = 5×10^6.

followups.q: Why must each pass be stable?
followups.a: LSD radix sorts by the least significant digit first and relies on earlier passes surviving inside ties of later ones. If the high-digit pass reordered equal high digits, it would destroy the low-digit ordering already established and the result would be wrong. Stability is not an optimisation here — it is the correctness argument.

followups.q: Where is the crossover, and what is the hidden cost?
followups.a: Radix is O(n) but pays 2 × 65536 counter slots and two full scatter passes with random writes. Below roughly 10^5 elements the bucket setup and cache misses lose to std::sort. It also needs an O(n) scratch buffer — 20 MB at n = 5×10^6 for uint32 — where std::sort is in-place. Uniform data favours radix; heavily skewed data leaves most buckets empty and narrows the gap.

items.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
items.statement: Per-element smaller-to-right counts. Solve BIT-route AND merge-route; merge must carry ORIGINAL indices.
hints: BIT: sweep right-to-left, record query before insert.
Merge route: when right wins, add left-segment length to its index's counter.

solutionCode.label: BIT sweeping right-to-left; query before insert

items.complexity: O(n log n) either way. Space O(n).

followups.a: The question is "how many elements to my right are smaller", so the BIT must contain exactly the elements to the right of i when i is processed. Sweeping backwards makes that true by construction. Querying before inserting keeps the element itself out of its own count.

followups.q: What does the merge route have to carry that plain inversion counting does not?
followups.a: Original indices. The answer is per-element, so when a right-half element wins the merge you must credit the remaining left-half count to the *specific original positions* of those left elements. Sorting (value, index) pairs and keeping the merge stable is what prevents the index bookkeeping from scrambling.

items.title: Reverse Pairs (harder inversions)
items.statement: Count i<j with a[i] > 2·a[j]. Condition no longer equals partition boundary — pre-merge pointer scan needed.
hints: Before merging halves, two-pointer j over sorted right half testing a[i] > 2*a[j].

solutionCode.label: count crossings in a separate scan, then merge normally

items.complexity: O(n log n) — a two-pointer counting scan plus a normal merge at every level. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why can this not be folded into the merge comparison like plain inversions?
followups.a: For ordinary inversions the counting condition (a[i] > a[j]) is exactly the merge's own comparison, so the count falls out for free. Here the condition is a[i] > 2·a[j], a different threshold — an element can satisfy the merge comparison but not the pair condition, or vice versa. The two scans must be separate, which is why this costs a second pass per level.

2*a[j] with a[j] near INT_MAX overflows a 32-bit int and wraps negative, making the comparison silently wrong. Writing 2LL forces 64-bit arithmetic. Python has arbitrary precision so the bug does not appear there — which is exactly why it is worth calling out in the C++ version.

items.title: Task Scheduler by Dual Keys (contest pattern)
items.statement: Sort tasks by (priority DESC, cost ASC, id ASC) via strict comparator; survive duplicate-flood stress test without RE.
hints: Local fuzz: 10⁵ equal-key elements through sort.

solutionCode.label: tie-chained strict comparator, never <= on any key

items.complexity: O(n log n). The comparator must be a strict weak ordering or std::sort exhibits undefined behaviour on ties.

followups.q: Why must the last key still be strict?
followups.a: If the final tiebreak returns `a.id <= b.id`, then two records with identical ids each compare "less than" the other. That breaks irreflexivity and asymmetry, and libstdc++ uses the comparator as a partition loop guard — the pointer runs off the array. A duplicate-flood test is the only thing that reliably detonates it.

followups.q: Why compare `!=` before returning the ordering on each key?
followups.a: Returning `a.priority > b.priority` unconditionally would report false for equal priorities and stop the chain there, so cost and id would never be consulted — the sort would be by priority alone with arbitrary tie order. The equality test is what makes the chain fall through rather than short-circuit.

items.title: K-th Smallest Pair Distance
items.statement: k-th smallest |a[i]−a[j]| among pairs. Sort once; binary search the DISTANCE value with sliding-window counting.
hints: Sorted array ⇒ pairs within distance d counted by window sweep.
Monotone count(d) ⇒ binary search smallest d with count ≥ k.
Full BS-on-answer doctrine arrives next module — this is your bridge.

solutionCode.label: binary search the DISTANCE, count pairs with a sliding window

items.complexity: O(n log n + n log W) — sort once, then binary search the distance range W with an O(n) window count per probe.

followups.q: Why is the answer space searchable rather than the array?
followups.a: count_at_most(d) is monotone non-decreasing in d — widening the threshold can never lose pairs. So the predicate "count ≥ k" is false then true, and you are looking for the boundary. You are binary searching over candidate answers, not over positions, which is the whole bs-on-answer pattern.

followups.q: Why does the window counter add `hi - lo` rather than 1?
followups.a: Once lo is the leftmost index with a[hi] − a[lo] ≤ d, every index in [lo, hi) pairs with hi inside the threshold — that is hi − lo pairs discovered in one step. Adding 1 would count only the nearest pair and undercount badly; the batching is what keeps the counter O(n).
